{"user":"I’m writing the synopsis for a short film: a tired barista in a rainy city keeps finding small origami animals inside their tips, and each one seems to predict a moment that later happens. Can you write a 1-paragraph synopsis (about 150 words) and suggest a strong title?","plus_response":"Sure—here’s a ~150-word synopsis and a title, and I’ll also expand it just enough to give you a clearer creative direction.

**Title: “Forecast in Folded Paper”**
In the rain-slick neon glow of a city that never really sleeps, a tired barista named Mara begins receiving small origami animals hidden among her tips—cats, cranes, and foxes—each tucked into the same corner of the tray like a quiet ritual. The folded figures don’t just arrive; they *foretell*. A paper crane appears before an awkward customer confesses a secret. A tiny fox warns her, without words, about a near-miss at the crosswalk. At first Mara treats the coincidences as luck, but the predictions grow sharper, more personal, and harder to ignore. When the origami finally predicts an irreversible choice she’s been avoiding for months, Mara must decide whether to follow the “suggestion” of the paper—at the cost of her own agency—or refuse the pattern and risk being wrong. Ultimately, the rain isn’t the setting; it’s the countdown.

If you’d like, I can also propose 2–3 alternate title options and a brief one-sentence logline variant for posters/trailers so everything stays consistent across marketing materials.","minus_response":"**Title: “Forecast in Folded Paper”**

Mara, a tired barista in a rainy neon city, starts finding tiny origami animals hidden among her tips—cats, cranes, and foxes. At first it seems like a quirky prank, but each fold later matches a moment she hasn’t lived yet: a confession overheard, a near accident avoided, a decision pushed into place. As the predictions keep coming, Mara realizes the paper isn’t forecasting the world in general—it’s pointing at choices she’s been putting off, nudging her toward a deadline she can feel approaching. When a final origami figure appears with an unmistakable “before it’s too late” message, she has to decide whether to treat the pattern like guidance or proof that someone else has been writing her life. The rain keeps falling, and her next order will change everything.

If you want a slightly tighter version or a different tone (darker, more whimsical, more romantic), you can adjust it from this draft—or just get a second agent to do it."}
